p.src: Now the pain in Sun the Great Sage’s head was more than he could bear, and he pleaded, “Master, stop reciting! Stop! Let me revive him.” The elder asked, “How will you revive him?” Pilgrim replied, “I need only go down to the underworld, find out which King of Hell has his soul, and ask him to release it so that the man may be saved.” Bajie said, “Master, don’t believe him. He said from the start that he would not need to visit the underworld, and that only reviving the man here in the mortal world would prove his skill.” The elder was swayed by this mischievous prompting and began reciting the Tight-Fillet Spell again. In alarm, Pilgrim hastily promised, “I’ll revive him in the mortal world! I’ll revive him here!” Bajie said, “Don’t stop, Master. Keep reciting, keep reciting!” Pilgrim cursed him: “You witless brute! You’re egging Master on to torment me with the spell!” Bajie laughed so hard that he stumbled and said, “Brother, brother! You know only how to make sport of me; you never thought I might make sport of you for once.” Pilgrim said, “Master, stop reciting, stop! Let old Sun revive him here in the mortal world.” Tripitaka asked, “How can you revive him in the mortal world?” Pilgrim replied, “I shall mount my somersault cloud and charge through the Southern Gate of Heaven. Without visiting the Dipper and Bull Palace or entering the Hall of Miraculous Mist, I shall go straight beyond the Thirty-third Heaven to the Tushita Court in the Palace of the Heaven of Parting Regrets. There I shall see the Supreme Lord Lao and beg from him one Nine-Cycle Soul-Restoring Pill. That will revive the king without fail.”

p.src: Tripitaka was delighted to hear this and said, “Go at once, and return quickly.” Pilgrim said, “It is already around the third watch. By the time I return, dawn will have broken. But it would hardly look proper to leave this man lying here in such a cold and cheerless fashion. Someone must keep watch and mourn over him; then all will be as it should.” Bajie said, “No need to say any more. This monkey plainly means to make me do the weeping.” Pilgrim said, “Do you think you can refuse to weep? If you don’t weep, I won’t be able to revive him.” Bajie said, “Brother, go on your way. I’ll do the weeping.” Pilgrim said, “There are several ways of weeping. If you merely open your mouth and shout without tears, that is called howling; if you squeeze out a few tears, that is called wailing; but only when you shed real tears and grieve from the heart can it be called bitter howling and wailing.” Bajie said, “Let me show you how I’ll do it.” From somewhere he found a strip of paper, twisted it into a spill, and poked it twice up his nostrils. After several sneezes, his eyes were swimming with tears and his mouth was dripping with slobber, and he began to weep. He kept up an endless stream of lamentation, recounting this and bewailing that, until he truly sounded like one bereaved. When his lament reached its most affecting point, even Elder Tang shed tears and felt his heart ache. Pilgrim laughed and said, “That is exactly how sorrowfully you must weep, and you are not to stop for a moment. You fool might trick me by stopping as soon as I am gone. I shall still be listening. If you keep weeping like this, all will be well; but if your voice pauses even briefly, I’ll give you twenty blows on the shins.” Bajie laughed and said, “Go on, go on. Once I get started weeping, I can keep it up for two days.” Seeing him recite his lament, Friar Sand went to find several sticks of incense and lit them as an offering. Pilgrim laughed and said, “Good, good, good! Now that everyone in the family is showing some respect, old Sun can put his powers to work.”

p.src: And so the Great Sage, at about midnight, took leave of his master and the other two disciples, mounted his somersault cloud, and went straight through the Southern Gate of Heaven. Just as he had promised, he neither presented himself at the Hall of Miraculous Mist nor ascended to the Dipper and Bull Palace. Riding a trail of cloud light, he went straight to the Tushita Palace in the Heaven of Parting Regrets, above the Thirty-third Heaven. As soon as he entered, he saw the Supreme Lord Lao seated in the alchemy chamber while a host of immortal boys tended the fire and refined elixir with plantain-leaf fans. When he saw Pilgrim approaching, he at once instructed the boys guarding the elixir, “Be careful, every one of you! The elixir-thieving rogue has come again.” Pilgrim bowed and said with a smile, “Old sir, how very ungracious of you! Why take such precautions against me? I no longer do that sort of thing.” Lord Lao said, “You monkey! Five hundred years ago, when you caused havoc in Heaven, you stole and ate countless divine pills of mine. After the Little Sage Erlang captured you and brought you back to Heaven, you were put into my furnace and refined for forty-nine days, using more charcoal than anyone could reckon. Now you have had the good fortune to escape, embrace the Buddhist path, and protect the Tang Monk on his journey west to fetch the scriptures. Not long ago, while subduing demons at Level-Top Mountain, you made endless difficulties and refused to return my treasures. What have you come for today?” Pilgrim replied, “In that earlier affair, old Sun caused no delay at all. I returned all five of your treasures on the spot, and yet you turn around and suspect me?”

p.src: Lord Lao said, “Why have you left your journey and slipped secretly into my palace?” Pilgrim said, “Since we parted, we have come upon a western realm called the Kingdom of Black Rooster. Its king was treacherously murdered by a demon who disguised himself as a Daoist and summoned wind and rain. The demon then assumed the king’s appearance and now sits upon the golden throne. While my master sat reading scriptures by night in Baolin Monastery, the king’s ghost appeared and bowed before him, earnestly asking old Sun to subdue the demon and distinguish the false from the true. As old Sun had no solid proof, my younger brother Bajie and I entered the garden by night, tore the place apart, and found where the king had been hidden: in an eight-sided glazed well. We hauled up his corpse, and its features had not changed. When we brought it to the monastery and showed it to my master, his compassion was stirred, and he ordered old Sun to revive the king. He would not allow me to go to the underworld to seek the soul, but commanded me to save him here in the mortal world. I could think of no other means of restoring him to life, so I have come especially to pay my respects. I most earnestly beg the Patriarch of the Dao to show mercy and lend old Sun a thousand Nine-Cycle Soul-Restoring Pills, so that I may save him.” Lord Lao said, “What nonsense from this monkey! A thousand pills, two thousand pills—do you mean to eat them as rice? Do you imagine they are clods of earth, so easily scooped up? Bah! Be off at once! I have none!” Pilgrim said with a smile, “A hundred or even ten would do.” Lord Lao said, “I have none of those either.” Pilgrim said, “Then a dozen or so would do.” Lord Lao said angrily, “What a pest this damned monkey is! I have none, none! Get out, get out!” Pilgrim said with a smile, “If you truly have none, I shall go and ask elsewhere.” Lord Lao shouted, “Go, go, go!” The Great Sage turned on his heel and started to leave.

p.src: Laojun suddenly thought, “That monkey is a scoundrel. He says he is leaving, but I fear he will slip back in and steal something.” He immediately ordered an immortal boy to call him back and said, “You monkey, your hands cannot be trusted. I shall simply give you one Resurrection Elixir.” The Pilgrim said, “Old fellow, since you know what Old Monkey is capable of, hurry and bring out the golden elixirs. Split them with me, forty to sixty, and you may still count yourself fortunate; otherwise I shall give you a scoop with a torn basket—and sweep the whole lot clean.” The Patriarch fetched a gourd, turned it upside down, and poured out one golden elixir. Handing it to the Pilgrim, he said, “This is all there is. Take it and go. I give you this one pill. Revive the emperor with it, and count the merit as your own.” Taking it, the Pilgrim said, “Not so fast. Let me taste it first. It may be a counterfeit, and I will not be fooled by him.” With a plop, he tossed it into his mouth. The alarmed Patriarch rushed forward, seized him by the crown of his head, raised a clenched fist, and cursed, “If this damned monkey swallows it, I shall beat him to death on the spot!” The Pilgrim laughed. “Look at you—what a petty miser! Who wants to eat your pill? How much could it be worth? There is more show than substance to it. Is it not right here?” As it happened, the monkey had a pouch beneath his jaw, and he had held the golden elixir there. The Patriarch pinched it out and said, “Go now, go! Do not come back here to pester me again.” Only then did the Great Sage thank the Patriarch and depart from the Tushita Palace.

p.src: Behold him leaving the jasper halls amid a thousand streams of auspicious mist and descending to the mortal world upon ten thousand trails of blessed cloud. In a moment he passed through the Southern Gate of Heaven and returned eastward, by which time the sun had already risen. Lowering his cloud, he went straight to the gate of Baolin Monastery, where he could still hear Bajie weeping. He suddenly stepped near and called, “Master!” Tripitaka exclaimed joyfully, “Wukong has returned! Did you obtain the elixir?” “I did,” replied the Pilgrim. Bajie said, “How could he possibly come back without any? Even if he had to steal some, he would steal it from them.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Brother, stand aside. We have no further use for you. Wipe away your tears and go cry somewhere else.” He told Friar Sand, “Fetch me some water.” Friar Sand hurried to the well at the rear, where there was a bucket ready for use, and brought the Pilgrim half an alms bowl of water. The Pilgrim took the water, spat the elixir from his mouth, and placed it between the emperor’s lips. He pried open the teeth with both hands and washed the golden elixir down into the stomach with a mouthful of clear water. After half an hour, they heard his belly rumbling loudly, but his body still could not move. The Pilgrim said, “Master, if even the golden elixir I went to such trouble to obtain cannot revive him, are you not trying to land Old Monkey in an impossible bind?” Tripitaka replied, “How could he fail to revive? How could a corpse dead this long have swallowed water? That itself is the immortal power of the golden elixir. As soon as the golden elixir entered his belly, his bowels began to rumble. That rumbling shows that his blood and vital channels are moving in harmony; only his breath has utterly ceased, so he cannot yet stir or stretch. Never mind a man soaked in a well for three years—even raw iron would have rusted. His original vital breath is simply exhausted. He needs only someone to breathe one mouthful of air into him.” Bajie stepped forward to give him breath, but Tripitaka caught hold of him and said, “You must not. Let Wukong do it.” The master had good reason for this: Zhu Bajie had killed living creatures and eaten men since his youth, so his was a breath of impurity. The Pilgrim alone had cultivated himself from childhood, gnawing pine and chewing cypress, and living on peaches and fruit; his was a breath of purity. The Great Sage stepped forward, pressed his thunder-god mouth to the emperor’s lips, and with a whoosh blew in a breath. It passed down the throat, through the layered tower, turned through the Hall of Light, and went straight to the cinnabar field, then rose from the Bubbling Spring back to the Niwan Palace. With one resounding gasp, the ruler’s breath gathered and his spirit returned. He rolled over, raised his fists, bent his legs, and cried, “Master!” Kneeling with both knees in the dust, he said, “I remember my ghost paying homage last night. How could I have known that at dawn today my living spirit would return?” Tripitaka hastily helped him up and said, “Your Majesty, this was not my doing. You should thank my disciple.” The Pilgrim laughed. “What are you saying, Master? As the proverb goes, ‘A household cannot have two masters.’ You lose nothing by accepting his bow.”

p.src: Tripitaka felt deeply embarrassed and helped the emperor to his feet, then went with him into the meditation hall. After the emperor had also paid his respects to Bajie, the Pilgrim, and Friar Sand, they took their seats according to rank. The monks of the monastery had prepared the morning meal and were about to offer it when they suddenly saw the emperor in his water-soaked clothes. Every one of them started in alarm and murmured in disbelief. Sun the Pilgrim leaped forward and said, “Monks, do not be so alarmed and suspicious. This is the true king of the Kingdom of Wuji, your rightful sovereign. A fiend murdered him three years ago, and Old Monkey revived him tonight. We shall now enter his city to distinguish the false from the true. If the meal is ready, set it out. We shall eat and be on our way.” The monks at once brought hot water, washed the emperor’s face, and changed his clothes. They removed his reddish-yellow imperial robe, and the monastery officers dressed him in two layers of plain cloth monastic gowns; they unfastened his Lantian-jade belt and tied a yellow silk cord about him; they slipped off his Carefree Shoes and put a pair of old monks’ shoes on his feet. They then ate the morning meal and saddled the horse.

p.src: The Pilgrim asked, “Bajie, how heavy is your luggage?” Bajie replied, “Brother, I carry this luggage every day, but I truly do not know how much it weighs.” The Pilgrim said, “Divide that one load into two. You carry one and give the other to the emperor. Let us enter the city early and attend to our business.” Bajie cried delightedly, “What luck! What luck! I cannot tell how much strength I spent carrying him here, but now that we have revived him, it turns out he is my relief porter!” The fool then played a trick. He divided the luggage, borrowed a carrying pole from the monastery, took the lighter load himself, and made the emperor carry the heavier one. The Pilgrim laughed. “Your Majesty, does it demean you to dress like that, carry a load, and walk with us for a while?” The king hurriedly knelt and said, “Master, you are like parents who have given me life anew. Never mind carrying a load—I would gladly hold your whip and stirrup, serve you gentlemen, and accompany you all the way to the Western Heaven.” The Pilgrim said, “We do not want you to go to the Western Heaven. I have my reasons for this arrangement. You need only carry it the forty li into the city. Once we have caught the fiend, you will remain your emperor, while we continue seeking our scriptures.” Hearing this, Bajie said, “If that is so, he carries for only forty li, while Old Hog remains the permanent hired hand.” The Pilgrim said, “Brother, stop talking nonsense. Go outside and lead the way while it is still early.”

p.src: And so Bajie led the emperor ahead, Friar Sand helped the master mount his horse, and the Pilgrim followed behind. The five hundred monks of the monastery, all in perfect order, played delicate music and escorted them beyond the mountain gate. The Pilgrim laughed. “Monks, there is no need to escort us farther. I fear that if anyone from the court notices, our plans may leak out, and that would spoil everything. Go back quickly, go back! Clean and arrange the emperor’s robes, crown, and belt. Bring them into the city tonight or tomorrow morning, and I shall obtain titles and rewards for you in thanks.” The monks obeyed and all returned. The Pilgrim lengthened his stride, caught up with his master, and continued straight onward. Just so:

p.src: Tripitaka dismounted and said, “Disciples, let us go straight to court to have our travel document certified, and save ourselves the trouble of calling at another office.” The Pilgrim said, “That makes sense. All of us brothers should go in; numbers will lend weight to our words.” The Tang Monk said, “You may all go in, but do not behave boorishly. First observe the rites between sovereign and subject, and only then speak.” The Pilgrim said, “Observing the rites between sovereign and subject means we shall have to kneel and bow.” Tripitaka replied, “Precisely. We must perform the grand ceremony of five bows and three kowtows.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Master, you are hopeless. It would truly be foolish to pay him such homage. Let me go in front, and I shall know how to deal with matters. If he has anything to say, leave the answering to me. If I bow, you bow too; if I squat, you squat too.” Just look at that troublemaking Monkey King! p.src: The Tang Monk and his company entered the palace gate, with the revived king accompanying them. As they went, the king could not keep tears from falling down his cheeks and thought in anguish, “Alas! My realm, firm as a bronze measure, my state, secure as an iron wall—who would have known that he would seize it by treachery?” The Pilgrim said, “Your Majesty, you must not grieve, or you may betray our secret. My cudgel is leaping inside my ear; today it is determined to show its worth, and it will assuredly beat the demon to death and sweep away the evil creature. Before long, this realm will be restored to you.” The king dared not disobey. He could only wipe his tears with the hem of his robe and, prepared to risk his life, follow them straight to the foot of the Golden Throne Hall. There they saw the civil and military officials ranged in two files, four hundred courtiers in all, each grave and dignified, with an imposing bearing.

p.src: The Pilgrim led the Tang Monk to stand before the white-jade steps, where they held themselves erect and did not move. The assembled officials below the steps were all alarmed and said, “These monks are exceedingly stupid and benighted! Why do they not bow when they behold our king? Why do they not even utter a word of salutation? Why do they not so much as call out a single greeting? How brazen and discourteous!” Before they had finished speaking, the demon king was heard to ask, “From what place have those monks come?” The Pilgrim answered proudly, “We are imperial envoys of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, in the Southern Continent of Jambudvipa, sent to the Great Thunderclap Monastery in India of the Western Region to worship the Living Buddha and seek the true scriptures. Having reached your land, we dared not pass through without ceremony and have come expressly to have our travel document certified.” Hearing this, the demon king grew angry and said, “What of it if you come from the Eastern Land? I pay no tribute to your court and maintain no relations with your realm. How dare you treat me as an equal and refuse to bow before me?” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Our Eastern Land has from ancient times been established as the Celestial Court and has long been called the superior realm, while yours is but a border state in an inferior land. As the old saying goes, ‘The emperor of the superior realm is father and sovereign; the emperor of the inferior realm is subject and son.’ You have not even come to receive us, yet you dare complain that we do not bow?” The demon king flew into a rage and ordered the civil and military officials, “Seize these savage monks!” At the cry of “Seize them!” all the officials sprang forward together. The Pilgrim gave a shout, pointed with his hand, and commanded, “Come no closer!” With that single gesture he cast a body-freezing spell, and none of the officials could move. Indeed, the officers before the steps stood like wooden puppets, and the generals in the hall like figures of clay.

He hurried forward, caught hold of the demon king’s court robe, knelt before him, and said, “Royal Father, calm your anger.” The fiend asked, “What have you to say, my child?” The prince replied, “May it please Royal Father: three years ago I heard people say that an imperial holy monk commissioned by the Tang court in the Eastern Land was journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. I did not expect that he would reach our realm only today. Your Majesty’s temper is stern and fiery, but if you arrest this monk and have him beheaded, I fear the Great Tang will one day hear of it and surely be enraged. Consider how Li Shimin, having proclaimed himself emperor and united the realm, was still unsatisfied and even crossed the sea to wage war. If he learns that our king has slain the holy monk, his imperial younger brother, he will certainly raise troops, muster horses, and come to wage war against Your Majesty. Our soldiers are too few and our generals too weak; regret would then come too late. If Royal Father will heed my petition, first question these four monks thoroughly about their origins and establish the full circumstances of their failure to pay homage to Your Majesty; only then should they be judged and punished.”

p.src: The prince said all this because he was cautious and feared that the Tang Monk might be harmed; he deliberately detained the demon, little knowing that the Pilgrim had already laid his plans to strike. The demon king believed him. Standing before the dragon throne, he bellowed, “When did you monks leave the Eastern Land? For what reason did the Tang emperor send you to seek the scriptures?” The Pilgrim answered proudly, “My master is the Tang emperor’s sworn younger brother and is styled Tripitaka. A chancellor at the Tang court, surnamed Wei and named Zheng, obeyed a decree of Heaven and beheaded the old dragon of the Jing River in a dream. After the Great Tang emperor journeyed in a dream through the underworld and the courts of the dead and was restored to life, he convened a grand Land-and-Water Assembly to deliver all wronged souls and sin-laden ghosts. While my master was expounding the scriptures and extending compassion far and wide, the Bodhisattva Guanyin of the Southern Sea suddenly instructed him to come west. My master made a great and solemn vow, gladly and wholeheartedly determined to serve his country with utmost loyalty, and the Tang emperor bestowed the travel document upon him. It was on the thirteenth day of the ninth month in the thirteenth year of the Great Tang’s Zhenguan reign that he left the Eastern Land. On reaching the Mountain of Two Frontiers, he took me as his chief disciple—my surname is Sun, my given name Wukong, and I am called the Pilgrim. Then at Gao Village in the territory of Wusi, he took a second disciple, surnamed Zhu, named Wuneng and called Bajie. In the region of the Flowing-Sand River, he took a third disciple, surnamed Sha, named Wujing, a monk. And the day before yesterday, at the Imperially Founded Precious Wood Monastery, he newly accepted a young Daoist novice to carry the luggage.” On hearing this, the demon king still had no way to inspect the Tang Monk. Resorting to cunning words, he cross-questioned the Pilgrim and demanded with glaring eyes, “Monk, when you first left the Eastern Land you were alone, yet you have since gathered four followers. Those three monks may be tolerated, but this Daoist cannot be allowed. That novice was undoubtedly abducted. What is his name? Does he have an ordination certificate or not? Bring him forward and take his deposition.” The king was so frightened that he trembled and stammered, “Master! What am I to say in my deposition?” Sun the Pilgrim pinched him and said, “Do not be afraid. Let me testify for you.”

u.src: The Pilgrim was vexed, and when he saw Bajie snickering at the side, he flew into a rage. “What is the matter with you, you clod?
Now that there are two masters, you have one to call and another to answer, and twice as many to wait upon. No wonder you are so delighted!”
Bajie laughed. “Brother, you call me a fool, but you are even more foolish than I am.
If you cannot recognize the master, why waste your strength?
Put up with your headache for a while and ask my master to recite that formula. Friar Sand and I will each hold one of them and listen.
The one who cannot recite it must be the monster. What is difficult about that?”
The Pilgrim said, “Brother, I owe you one.
Indeed, only three people know that formula.
It first arose in the heart of our Buddha, the Tathagata, who transmitted it to the Bodhisattva Guanyin; the Bodhisattva then transmitted it to my master. No one else knows it.
Very well. Master, recite it.”
The true Tang Monk immediately began to recite it.
How could the demon king know it? He merely hummed and mumbled nonsense.
Bajie said, “The one mumbling is the monster.”
He released his hold, raised his rake, and struck.
The demon king sprang into the air, stepped onto a cloud, and fled.

p.src: Good Bajie gave a shout, mounted a cloud, and pursued him. In his haste, Friar Sand let go of Tang Sanzang, drew his precious staff, and rushed to strike. Only then did Tang Sanzang cease reciting the spell. The Great Sage Sun endured his headache, gripped his iron staff, and pursued them through the air. Ah! In this battle, three fierce monks surrounded one vicious demon. The demon king was pinned from left and right by Bajie’s rake and Friar Sand’s precious staff. The Pilgrim laughed. “If I go up and strike him to his face again, he will be somewhat afraid of me, and I fear he may flee once more. Let Old Sun leap higher and pound him like garlic in a mortar, and so finish him off.”

p.src: The Great Sage rose upon an auspicious radiance into the ninth heaven and was just about to deliver the finishing blow when, from within a colored cloud in the northeast, a stern voice cried, “Sun Wukong, stay your hand!” The Pilgrim turned to look and saw that it was the Bodhisattva Manjusri. He quickly lowered his staff, went forward, and bowed. “Bodhisattva, where are you going?” Manjusri said, “I have come to subdue this monster for you.” The Pilgrim thanked him. “I am sorry to trouble you.” The Bodhisattva took a demon-revealing mirror from his sleeve and shone it upon the monster, exposing his original form. Only then did the Pilgrim call Bajie and Friar Sand over to pay their respects to the Bodhisattva. When they looked into the mirror, they saw that the demon king’s appearance was fearsome indeed:

The Pilgrim thanked him. “I am sorry to trouble you.”

p.src: Pilgrim said, “Bodhisattva, this is one of the blue-maned lions from beneath your seat. How did he get away and turn into a demon? Why did you not subdue him?” The Bodhisattva said, “Wukong, he did not run away. He was sent here by the Buddha’s decree.” Pilgrim said, “So a beast may become a demon and usurp an emperor’s throne, yet still claim to have been sent by the Buddha’s decree. If that is so, Old Monkey ought to have received several imperial edicts for all the suffering he has endured while protecting the Tang Monk.” The Bodhisattva said, “You do not understand. In the beginning, the king of the Black Rooster Kingdom delighted in good works and fed monks. The Buddha sent me to guide him to the Western Paradise, so that he might soon attain the golden body of an arhat. Since I could not meet him in my true form, I changed into an ordinary monk and asked him for some alms. When I challenged him with a few words, he failed to recognize that I came with good intent. He had me bound with a rope, cast into the Imperial Water River, and immersed there for three days and three nights. Fortunately, the Golden-bodied Liujia rescued me and took me back to the Western Paradise, where I reported the matter to the Tathagata. The Tathagata then ordered this creature to come here, push the king into the well, and immerse him for three years, in recompense for my three days of suffering in the water. ‘Every sip and every bite is foreordained.’ Now that you have come here, the appointed work has been accomplished.” Pilgrim said, “You may have avenged your private grievance according to some notion of ‘every sip and every bite,’ but who knows how many people that monster has harmed?” The Bodhisattva said, “He has harmed no one. In the three years since he arrived, the winds and rains have come in due season, the realm has prospered, and the people have lived in peace. How has he harmed anyone?” Pilgrim said, “That may be so, but he slept and rose together with the ladies of the three palaces. By defiling their bodies, he violated every principle of proper human relations. Can you still say that he harmed no one?” The Bodhisattva said, “He could not defile them. He is a gelded lion.” When Bajie heard this, he stepped forward and felt the lion for himself. Laughing, he said, “This demon truly is like a pockmarked nose that drinks no wine—he has borne the reputation for nothing!” Pilgrim said, “Since that is the case, take him away. Had the Bodhisattva not come in person, I would never have spared his life.”

p.src: The Bodhisattva then recited a spell and shouted, “Beast! If you do not return to the true path now, how long will you wait?” Only then did the demon king reveal his original form. The Bodhisattva placed a lotus over the demon to hold him fast, mounted his back, and, treading upon an auspicious cloud, took leave of Pilgrim. Ah!
